Sensitivity analysis for the assumptions the data cannot check

Source: R/sensitivity.R
sensitivity_analysis.Rd

Shows how the accuracy of the tests changes with the two assumptions of the saturated model that the data cannot check: the odds ratio of verification between diseased and healthy subjects (set with verification = mnar() in the model) and the prior on the proportion of diseased in the never-verified profiles (Buzoianu and Kadane, 2008). For the saturated model no new fit is needed: these parameters do not enter the likelihood (Gustafson, 2015), so the draws of the identified parameters are reused and only the assumptions are changed.

Usage

sensitivity_analysis(
  fit,
  odds_ratios = NULL,
  unverified_priors = NULL,
  rules = NULL,
  level = 0.95,
  ...
)

Arguments

fit

A model fitted with baysesp().

odds_ratios

Values of the odds ratio of verification between diseased and healthy subjects, \(\exp(\beta)\); 1 is MAR. NULL keeps the assumption of the fitted model.

unverified_priors

List of alternative priors on the proportion of diseased in the never-verified profiles. Each element is a prior, or a list with one prior per never-verified profile. NULL keeps the prior of the fitted model.

rules

Rules, see rule_accuracy(). By default the individual tests, as in test_accuracy().

level

Probability of the credible intervals.

...

For the structured models, arguments passed to baysesp() for the new fits, such as chains and seed.

Value

A data frame with the columns odds_ratio (NA when it follows the prior of a model with verification = mnar()) and unverified_prior, which describe the assumptions, followed by the columns of test_accuracy() or rule_accuracy(), without identified.

Details

For the structured models (loglinear(), random_effects()) the odds ratio enters the likelihood, so the model is fitted again for each value, with the odds ratio fixed; the never-verified profiles have no separate prior to change.

The odds ratio is fixed at each value of odds_ratios: with a grid of values this is a tipping-point analysis, which shows at which odds ratio a conclusion changes (Kosinski and Barnhart, 2003b). With odds_ratios = NULL the odds ratio of the fitted model is kept (1 with verification = mar(), the prior odds_ratio_prior with verification = mnar()). The new priors in unverified_priors are sampled with the random number generator of R: set the seed for reproducible results.

Recomputation for the saturated model. The saturated model estimates, for each profile \(t\), its frequency \(\omega_t\), the fraction of verified subjects \(v_t\) and the proportion of diseased among them \(\phi^{(1)}_t\). With odds ratio of verification \(OR = \exp(\beta)\), the proportion of diseased among the unverified is \(\phi^{(0)}_t = \mathrm{expit}(\mathrm{logit}(\phi^{(1)}_t) - \beta)\): with \(OR > 1\) the unverified are less often diseased than the verified (Kosinski and Barnhart, 2003a). The proportion of diseased in the profile is then $$\psi_t = v_t\, \phi^{(1)}_t + (1 - v_t)\, \phi^{(0)}_t,$$ or \(\psi_t = q_t\), drawn from the prior, for a never-verified profile. From these, \(\pi = \sum_t \omega_t \psi_t\), \(\theta_{1,t} = \omega_t \psi_t / \pi\) and \(\theta_{0,t} = \omega_t (1 - \psi_t) / (1 - \pi)\), and the accuracy measures below.

The accuracy is defined for a rule \(R\), which declares a subject positive or negative from the response profile \(t\), the vector of the results of the tests: \(r_R(t) = 1\) if the profile is declared positive, 0 otherwise. A single test is the rule "this test is positive". The quantities depend on the prevalence \(\pi = P(D = 1)\) and on the distribution of the profiles in the diseased, \(\theta_{1,t} = P(T = t \mid D = 1)\), and in the healthy, \(\theta_{0,t} = P(T = t \mid D = 0)\):

  • sensitivity (Se): $$Se_R = P(R \textrm{ positive} \mid D = 1) = \sum_t r_R(t)\, \theta_{1,t},$$ the proportion of diseased subjects that the rule declares positive. It is also called the true positive rate (TPR);

  • specificity (Sp): $$Sp_R = P(R \textrm{ negative} \mid D = 0) = 1 - \sum_t r_R(t)\, \theta_{0,t},$$ the proportion of healthy subjects that the rule declares negative; \(1 - Sp_R\) is the false positive rate (FPR);

  • positive predictive value (PPV): $$PPV_R = P(D = 1 \mid R \textrm{ positive}) = \frac{\pi\, Se_R}{\pi\, Se_R + (1 - \pi)(1 - Sp_R)},$$ the probability that a subject declared positive is diseased;

  • negative predictive value (NPV): $$NPV_R = P(D = 0 \mid R \textrm{ negative}) = \frac{(1 - \pi)\, Sp_R}{(1 - \pi)\, Sp_R + \pi\, (1 - Se_R)},$$ the probability that a subject declared negative is healthy.

Sensitivity and specificity describe the rule and do not depend on the prevalence; the predictive values describe what a result means for a subject, and change with the prevalence of the population. For combined rules, such as any_positive(), the accuracy depends on the joint distribution of the tests, not only on their individual sensitivities and specificities (Torrance-Rynard and Walter, 1997; Vacek, 1985).

Each quantity is computed from every posterior draw of \(\pi\), \(\theta_0\) and \(\theta_1\). The results report its posterior mean and median and an equal-tailed credible interval with probability level.

References

Buzoianu, M. and Kadane, J. B. (2008). Adjusting for verification bias in diagnostic test evaluation: A Bayesian approach. Statistics in Medicine, 27(13), 2453–2473. doi:10.1002/sim.3099

Gustafson, P. (2015). Bayesian Inference for Partially Identified Models: Exploring the Limits of Limited Data. Chapman & Hall/CRC, Boca Raton, FL.

Kosinski, A. S. and Barnhart, H. X. (2003a). Accounting for nonignorable verification bias in assessment of diagnostic tests. Biometrics, 59(1), 163–171. doi:10.1111/1541-0420.00019

Kosinski, A. S. and Barnhart, H. X. (2003b). A global sensitivity analysis of performance of a medical diagnostic test when verification bias is present. Statistics in Medicine, 22(17), 2711–2721. doi:10.1002/sim.1517

Torrance-Rynard, V. L. and Walter, S. D. (1997). Effects of dependent errors in the assessment of diagnostic test performance. Statistics in Medicine, 16(19), 2157–2175. doi:10.1002/(SICI)1097-0258(19971015)16:19<2157::AID-SIM653>3.0.CO;2-X

Vacek, P. M. (1985). The effect of conditional dependence on the evaluation of diagnostic tests. Biometrics, 41(4), 959–968. doi:10.2307/2530967

Examples

# \donttest{
set.seed(1)
d <- simulate_study(n = 2000, prevalence = 0.2,
                    sensitivity = c(A = 0.9, B = 0.8),
                    specificity = c(A = 0.85, B = 0.95),
                    verification_prob = c(0.2, 0.9, 0.9, 1), odds_ratio = 2)
d <- baysesp_data(d, tests = c("A", "B"), verified = "verified", disease = "disease")
fit <- baysesp(d, seed = 1)
sensitivity_analysis(fit, odds_ratios = c(1, 1.5, 2, 3))
